title: Elara’s Orchard: Blight and Branching Choices

scenario.title: Elara’s Orchard: Blight and Branching Choices
scenario.setting: Elara’s Orchard is divided into 12 interconnected microcells: heirloom apple guild beds, mason bee nesting boxes, rain-harvest cisterns, and stone fruit barrier rows. Planted by their great-grandmother 13 years prior, it’s now sustained by three sibling stewards and a rotating crew of local volunteers, having cleared its first critical growth year and entered its second decade of production. The core dilemma hinges on the orchard’s original cider apple tree, whose root flare shows signs of neonatal blight, splitting the siblings over how best to save it.

characters.name: Mara
characters.tendencies: She curates the siblings' shared digital archive of great-grandma's orchard notes, cross-referencing weekly microcell surveys against Elara’s original planting plan. She refuses to consider untested treatments because she fears losing the orchard's original ancestral lineage.

characters.name: Lila
characters.tendencies: She’s spent the last three months trialing organic copper sulfate sprays on the affected tree, refining application rates to minimize harm to nearby pollinator habitats. She argues that delaying the experimental treatment will lead to the tree's death before the autumn harvest.

characters.name: Javi
characters.tendencies: He runs the orchard’s community-supported agriculture program, hosting monthly open houses and recruiting local volunteers to assist with daily maintenance. He worries that diverting all their resources to saving one tree will leave other parts of the orchard’s microcell network under-cared for.

characters.name: Kaelin
characters.tendencies: They’re a local teen volunteer who first discovered the orchard through Javi’s social media posts, and they’ve begun documenting the orchard’s unplanned volunteer saplings. They’ve noticed new shoots sprouting from the base of the blighted tree, and they advocate for letting natural regeneration lead the way.

turns.name: Mara
turns.text:
I just pulled the latest Microcell 4 soil moisture survey off the shared archive. I’m cross-referencing it against Elara’s formal planting plan to confirm we only use treatments great-grandma documented in her orchard notes. We can’t risk introducing untested additives that could disrupt this orchard’s original ancestral lineage.
[leans in to adjust the handheld tablet’s zoom to highlight the heirloom apple rootstock entries from 1927]

turns.name: Javi
turns.text:
I just checked in with the first volunteer shift, and most are focused on the ailing heritage walnut we’re all rallying to save. I can’t shake the worry that the mason bee nesting boxes in the western microcells haven’t been inspected in three weeks, so we need to carve out a small window tomorrow to split crews so no part of the orchard gets overlooked.
[grabs a stack of torn volunteer sign-up sheets from the wooden tool cart at his feet]

turns.name: Kaelin
turns.text:
I stopped by the blighted heirloom apple tree in the south microcell earlier and spotted tender new saplings sprouting from its root base. We should skip cutting it down entirely—these shoots will grow into healthy, fruiting trees with just a little space, and that’s exactly the unplanned natural regen I’ve been tracking for my project. It’s such a quiet, perfect win for the orchard.
[kneels to press a handwritten field tag next to the sapling cluster while scribbling a quick update in their spiral-bound notebook]

turns.name: Mara
turns.text:
I need to cross-reference those south microcell apple root shoots against great-grandma’s official propagation logs before we prioritize nurturing them—we can’t risk deviating from documented lineage practices. I also want to pull the western microcell mason bee nesting box placement records to address your earlier concern, to make sure we’re sticking to her specified spacing rules rather than adjusting things on the fly.
[reaches for the thick, leather-bound great-grandma orchard archive binder tucked under the shared worktable]

turns.name: Lila
turns.text:
Three months of trials have taught me exactly how little copper sulfate these trees can take before runoff threatens the western nesting boxes—my refined rates cut application volume by nearly half with no spike in bee activity loss. But blight doesn't wait for consensus, and every week we debate is a week closer to losing the walnut before autumn. I've documented every spray date, every dilution, every weather window; if we delay past this month, we might as well be sharpening the axe ourselves. Mara, my application logs are on the shared archive if you want to verify them against Elara's records yourself.

[unrolls her spray-log ledger across the planning table, tapping the color-coded application schedule]

turns.name: Javi
turns.text:
I can’t shake the worry that the western microcell’s mason bee nesting boxes are going completely unmaintained while all our volunteers focus on the ailing heritage walnut. We need to reassign a small crew to tend those boxes and check in on the south apple tree’s root saplings too. Let me pull up the volunteer rosters right now to rework today’s shifts.
[grabs the dog-eared volunteer shift clipboard from the tool shed counter]

turns.name: Kaelin
turns.text:
I stopped by the blighted heirloom apple tree in the south microcell earlier and spotted tender new saplings sprouting from its root base. We should skip cutting it down entirely—these shoots will grow into full, healthy apple trees in a few years, and I’ve been documenting every unplanned volunteer sapling across the orchard to track this kind of spontaneous regrowth.
[kneels down to gently tuck a stray clump of grass away from one of the tiny, bright green shoots]
